name: First Principles Thinking
oneSentence: Break a problem down to what you know is true, then rebuild from there.
definition: Reasoning from foundational truths rather than by analogy to how things are already done. Descartes resolved to doubt everything he could and rebuild only on what survived the doubting. The move is to strip a problem back to the things you can actually defend, then reason forward from those alone.
misconception: "It means ignoring what everyone else does." It does not require discarding convention. It requires knowing which parts of it are load-bearing. Most conventions encode a real constraint; the work is separating those from the ones that merely persist.
nearestNeighbour: CHESTERTON'S FENCE. That one warns you not to remove a convention until you understand why it exists. This one is the method for examining it. They pull in opposite directions and are strongest used together.
discriminateScenario: A caterer prices every job at twice her ingredient cost, because that is what her old employer did. When a large order loses money she sits down and works out what actually drives her costs, and finds that labour, not ingredients, is the thing her pricing should have been tracking all along.
praxisExercise:
STRIP IT DOWN

1. Name one rule you follow in your work.
2. Write down why you believe it is true.
3. For each reason ask: do I know this, or did I inherit it?
4. Keep only what you can defend, and rebuild the rule from those parts.

COMMITMENT (if-then):
"When I catch myself saying this is how it is done, I will write down what I actually know to be true before going further."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Inversion
oneSentence: Solve a problem backwards by asking what would guarantee failure.
definition: Rather than asking how to succeed, you ask how you would reliably fail, then remove those conditions. Attributed to the mathematician Carl Jacobi, who advised inverting difficult problems, and made a standing habit of thought by Charlie Munger.
misconception: "Inversion is just negative thinking." It is not pessimism. Failure conditions are simply easier to name precisely than success conditions, which is why inverting produces a list you can act on where the forward question produces platitudes.
nearestNeighbour: PREMORTEM. That one imagines a particular project has already failed and asks why. This is the general move of flipping any question on its head; the premortem is one applied instance of it.
discriminateScenario: Tom wants to write a book and keeps making plans that go nowhere. A friend asks him instead to list everything he could do to make sure he never finishes it. He names four things straight away, realises he is already doing three of them, and stops one that week.
praxisExercise:
FAILURE AUDIT

1. Choose one goal you currently care about.
2. Ask: how could I guarantee failure here?
3. List five behaviours that would make failure likely.
4. Mark the ones you are already doing.
5. Remove one of them this week.

COMMITMENT (if-then):
"When I set a goal, I will write the five ways I could guarantee failure before I write any plan."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Principle of Charity
oneSentence: Interpreting what someone said in its strongest reasonable sense.
definition: A principle of interpretation holding that when a statement admits of several readings, you should engage the one that is most coherent and most likely to be meant. It is not generosity for its own sake. A weak reading of an argument tells you nothing about whether the argument is any good, so charity is a condition of learning anything from disagreement.

chains: you take the weakest available reading
you learn nothing and they do not change
either you are changed or they are

misconception: "Being charitable means agreeing more, or being soft on bad arguments." It makes criticism harder to escape, not softer. Refuting the strongest version is a far more serious challenge than refuting a sloppy one, and the person cannot reply that you misunderstood them.
nearestNeighbour: STEELMANNING. That goes a step further and improves the argument beyond what was actually said, constructing the best possible case. Charity stays within what the person plausibly meant. One is accurate interpretation, the other is active reconstruction.
discriminateScenario: In a thread about remote work, someone writes that offices help junior staff. A reply treats this as a claim that everyone must return five days a week, and knocks it down easily. The original poster never meant that, and the exchange ends with both sides more certain than before.
praxisExercise:
THE BEST READING

1. Find something you disagreed with this week, in writing.
2. Write the reading of it you reacted to.
3. Write the strongest reading it could bear.
4. Decide whether your objection still holds against the second one.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I am about to disagree in writing, I will write the strongest version of their point first and check my objection against that."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Steelmanning
oneSentence: Building the strongest version of an argument before you take it apart.
definition: A practice of constructing the best case for a position, including improvements its actual defenders have not made, and then responding to that. Where charity asks you to read fairly, steelmanning asks you to build. Its purpose is partly honesty and partly self interest, because an objection that only defeats a weak version has told you nothing about whether you are right.

chains: you argue against what was said
any weakness in their phrasing does your work for you
your own position is never tested
you argue against the strongest possible version
their phrasing is no longer the weak point
you find out whether you are actually right

misconception: "Steelmanning is a debate tactic for looking fair minded." If it is performed rather than done, it is worthless. The point is private, not social: you build the strong version in order to find out whether your own view survives it, and sometimes it does not.
nearestNeighbour: PRINCIPLE OF CHARITY. That asks you to interpret what was said in its strongest reasonable sense, staying within what the person meant. This goes beyond them, improving the argument past anything they said. Charity is about accuracy, this is about construction.
discriminateScenario: Before writing a piece arguing against a popular productivity method, Nadia spends an afternoon writing the best case for it she can manage. Two of her four objections do not survive the exercise. The piece she eventually publishes makes the remaining two, and is far harder to dismiss.
praxisExercise:
BUILD IT FIRST

1. Take a position you argue against.
2. Write the best case for it you can, including points its defenders usually miss.
3. Show it to someone who holds that view and ask what you left out.
4. Now write your objection, against that version.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I plan to argue against something publicly, I will write its strongest case first and check which of my objections survive."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Straw Man Fallacy
oneSentence: Refuting a distorted version of an argument instead of the real one.
definition: An error of reasoning in which a position is restated in a weakened or exaggerated form, and the weakened form is then defeated. The appearance of victory comes from the substitution, not from the argument. It is often unintentional, since the distorted version is usually the one that felt easiest to answer.

chains: real claim is hard to answer
a simpler version comes to mind

misconception: "A straw man is just any unfair characterisation of someone's view." Unfairness alone is not enough. The error is specifically substituting a weaker claim and then treating its defeat as a defeat of the original. Describing someone's view rudely but accurately is not this.
nearestNeighbour: MOTTE AND BAILEY. That is the mirror image, where a speaker defends a modest claim and then behaves as though a far bolder one had been established. One distorts the opponent's position downward, the other shifts one's own position back and forth.
discriminateScenario: A councillor proposes reducing the speed limit on two residential streets. At the public meeting a resident stands up to say that banning cars from the town centre would destroy local business, and sits down to applause. The speed limit proposal is never discussed.
praxisExercise:
FIND THE SUBSTITUTION

1. Recall an argument you felt you won easily.
2. Write what you argued against.
3. Write what they actually claimed, in their words if you have them.
4. If the two differ, your win was against something you built.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When an opposing argument feels easy to defeat, I will check their actual words before replying."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Sunk-Cost Fallacy
oneSentence: Carrying on with something because of what you already spent on it.
definition: A sunk cost is a cost already paid that cannot be recovered. The fallacy is letting it influence a decision about the future. Rationally, only the costs and benefits still ahead of you should count; in practice, what has already gone in exerts a strong pull toward continuing.

chains: the decision is made on the past rather than the future

misconception: "It means you should quit things easily." It does not. Plenty of commitments are worth continuing on their own merits. The fallacy is specifically about using past expenditure as the reason, rather than whether the thing is still worth doing from here.
nearestNeighbour: LOSS AVERSION. That one is the general tendency to feel losses more sharply than equivalent gains. Sunk cost is a specific decision error that loss aversion helps explain. You can be loss averse without committing the fallacy, and the fallacy also draws on a reluctance to look inconsistent.
discriminateScenario: Elena is two years into a qualification she no longer wants, in a field she has decided against. Every time she considers stopping, she thinks about the fees and the evenings already spent. She signs up for another year, and cannot say what the qualification will actually get her.
praxisExercise:
THE FRESH START TEST

1. Name a commitment you are unsure about.
2. Ask: if I were arriving at this today, with none of the history, would I choose it?
3. If no, write what is actually keeping you in it.
4. Separate the reasons that look forward from the ones that look back.

COMMITMENT (if-then):
"When I notice I am justifying something by what I have already put in, I will ask what I would choose if I were starting from today."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Solomon’s Paradox
oneSentence: We reason more wisely about other people's problems than our own.
definition: Named for King Solomon, who counselled others wisely but governed his own household badly. Grossmann and Kross found that people reason about their own problems with measurably less wisdom, by which is meant acknowledging the limits of what they know, allowing for change, weighing other perspectives and seeking compromise, than about an identical problem belonging to someone else.
misconception: "People are just smarter about other people's lives." The effect is not about intelligence, and not about caring less. The same person, with the same intelligence, reasons worse on their own problem. The variable is distance, not ability, which is why manufacturing distance artificially reverses the effect.
nearestNeighbour: ACTOR-OBSERVER BIAS. That one is about attribution: we explain our own behaviour by circumstance and other people's by character. This is about the quality of reasoning itself, not about who gets blamed. A person can show either one without the other.
discriminateScenario: Maya tells her friend, without hesitating, that she should leave a relationship in which she is constantly let down. Six months later Maya is in a near-identical situation and finds herself explaining why this time the circumstances are different, and why leaving now would be premature.
praxisExercise:
THE OUTSIDER TEST

1. Choose one unresolved problem currently affecting you.
2. Write it in the third person: "[Name] has been struggling with..."
3. Answer as though advising your closest friend:
   - What would you tell her?
   - What is she failing to see?
   - What is she treating as certain that is not?
   - Whose perspective has she not considered?
   - What might look different in six months?
4. Return to the first person: what advice still applies to you?

COMMITMENT (if-then):
"When I notice I am emotionally invested in a decision, I will write the problem in the third person before deciding anything."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Gottman’s Four Horsemen
oneSentence: Four patterns in conflict that predict a relationship is in trouble.
definition: Gottman's observational work identified four communication patterns that reliably predict relationship breakdown: criticism, which attacks character rather than behaviour, contempt, which conveys superiority, defensiveness, which deflects responsibility, and stonewalling, which withdraws from the exchange altogether. Contempt was the strongest single predictor.

chains: the cycle repeats with nothing addressed

misconception: "It means couples who argue are in trouble." Arguing frequency was not what predicted anything. Stable couples argued plenty. What separated them was the absence of these four patterns inside the arguing, particularly contempt.
nearestNeighbour: DEMAND WITHDRAW PATTERN. That is one specific cycle where one partner pursues and the other retreats, and it maps closely onto two of the four, criticism and stonewalling. The four horsemen are a wider set of markers rather than a single interactional loop.
discriminateScenario: Every time the finances come up, one of them starts with you never and the other starts with well you are the one who. Within four minutes one has stopped responding and is looking at their phone. They have had this exact exchange perhaps thirty times and have never once discussed the actual budget.
praxisExercise:
SPOT YOUR OWN

1. Recall your last difficult conversation with someone close.
2. Of the four, which one did you supply? Be specific about the sentence.
3. Write what the behaviour based version of that sentence would have been.
4. Use it next time the subject arises.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I catch myself starting a sentence with you always or you never, I will stop and name the specific behaviour instead."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Active Listening
oneSentence: Listening to understand the person rather than to prepare your reply.
definition: A practice in which the listener's whole attention goes to building an accurate picture of what the speaker means, and the speaker can see that happening. It involves not interrupting, not rehearsing a response while the other person talks, and checking your understanding out loud before responding to it. Rogers and Farson set it out as a working method rather than a personality trait.

chains: you hear only the parts you can answer
the speaker feels understood and says more

misconception: "Active listening means nodding and saying mm hmm." Those are signals, not the practice. A person can nod continuously while composing their rebuttal. The practice is the internal act of trying to build their meaning rather than your answer, and the signals only matter if that is actually happening.
nearestNeighbour: REFLECTIVE LISTENING. That is one technique inside this practice, where you say back what you understood. Active listening is the wider posture of attending to meaning first, which can be shown in many ways besides reflecting.
discriminateScenario: Priya's colleague starts describing a problem with the schedule. Twenty seconds in, Priya has the answer and is waiting for a pause to say it. She delivers a good solution. Her colleague thanks her, and does not mention the part he had not got to yet, which was the actual difficulty.
praxisExercise:
THE NO REPLY MINUTE

1. Choose one conversation today that matters.
2. For the first minute, do not plan any part of your response.
3. When they pause, say what you understood before you say anything else.
4. Note afterwards: did they add something they had not said yet?

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When someone brings me a problem, I will say back what I understood before I offer anything."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Reflective Listening
oneSentence: Saying back what you understood, so the speaker can correct you.
definition: A technique in which the listener restates the speaker's meaning in their own words and invites correction. Its value is not politeness. It converts a private, unverified guess about what someone meant into something they can confirm or fix, which is the only way to know whether you understood.

chains: you respond to the wrong thing
you say the interpretation out loud
you respond to what they meant

misconception: "It means repeating their words back to them." Repeating the words proves nothing, since you can parrot a sentence you have not understood. It has to be in your own words, because the act of rephrasing is what exposes whether you actually got it.
nearestNeighbour: ACTIVE LISTENING. That is the wider practice of attending to meaning rather than to your reply. This is one specific move inside it, and you can do this move badly while listening well, or do it mechanically while listening poorly.
discriminateScenario: A client writes a long message about wanting things to move faster. Tom replies with a revised timeline. She writes back that speed was not really the issue, it was that she had not known where things stood. Tom had solved the problem he recognised rather than the one she had.
praxisExercise:
SAY IT BACK

1. Pick a conversation where you and the other person keep missing each other.
2. Before responding, say: so what I am hearing is, and then put their point in your own words.
3. Ask whether that is right.
4. Write down what they corrected. That difference is what you had been answering.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When a conversation feels like it is going in circles, I will restate their point in my own words and ask if I have it."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Affect Labeling
oneSentence: Naming an emotion out loud reduces its intensity.
definition: Putting a feeling into words measurably lowers its grip, in yourself and in the person you are speaking to. Lieberman's imaging work found that labelling an emotion reduced activity in the amygdala and raised it in regions associated with deliberate control. In conversation it means naming what the other person appears to feel rather than arguing with it.

chains: it becomes a specific thing on the table
it can be discussed instead of acted out

misconception: "You are telling people how they feel." The move is tentative, not declarative. It is closer to it sounds like this has been frustrating than to you are frustrated. Getting it slightly wrong still works, because the person corrects you and has now named it themselves.
nearestNeighbour: COGNITIVE REAPPRAISAL. That one changes how you interpret a situation in order to change the feeling. This one does not reinterpret anything. It simply names the feeling as it is, and the naming alone does the work.
discriminateScenario: A customer has been escalating for ten minutes. Instead of restating the refund policy again, the agent says it sounds like the worst part was being passed between three people. The customer stops, agrees, and the volume drops. Nothing about the policy has changed.
praxisExercise:
NAME IT FIRST

1. Choose a conversation you expect to be tense.
2. Before addressing the content, name what the other person seems to be feeling, tentatively.
3. Let them correct you if you are off.
4. Only then move to the substance.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When someone is clearly upset, I will name what they seem to be feeling before I address the facts."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Open Ended Questions
oneSentence: Questions that cannot be answered yes or no, so the other person chooses what matters.
definition: A question built so the answer has to be constructed rather than selected. Closed questions test a hypothesis you already have. Open questions hand the choice of direction to the other person, which is how you find out the thing you did not know to ask about.

chains: they confirm or deny your guess
you learn only about your guess
you learn what you did not know to ask

misconception: "Open questions are just longer questions." Length has nothing to do with it. Tell me more is open and short. Did the delay frustrate you is closed and long. What makes a question open is whether the shape of the answer is already decided by the asker.
nearestNeighbour: ELABORATIVE INTERROGATION. That is a study technique where you ask yourself why a fact is true in order to remember it. This is a conversational move aimed at another person, with the purpose of discovery rather than retention.
discriminateScenario: A manager asks each person leaving the company whether they were happy with their pay. Almost all say yes, and she concludes pay is not the problem. She never finds out that three of them left because of the same colleague, because nothing she asked left room for it.
praxisExercise:
THE QUESTION SWAP

1. Write the three questions you plan to ask in your next important conversation.
2. For each, ask whether you could answer it yourself with a guess.
3. If you could, rewrite it so you could not.
4. Ask the rewritten versions.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I prepare questions for a conversation that matters, I will rewrite any I could already guess the answer to."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Grice’s Cooperative Principle
oneSentence: Conversation runs on an unspoken agreement to be informative, truthful, relevant and clear.
definition: Grice proposed that conversation is governed by a cooperative principle and four maxims: say enough but not too much, say what you believe true, say what is relevant, and say it clearly. The maxims are not rules people obey. They are expectations that let a listener work out what is meant from what is said, including when a maxim is deliberately broken.

chains: listener assumes the speaker is cooperating
speaker says something that seems to break a maxim
listener infers the meaning that would restore cooperation
more is communicated than was said

misconception: "The maxims are rules for how to speak well." Grice was describing how understanding works, not giving advice. The interesting cases are the ones where a maxim is flouted on purpose, since that is precisely how sarcasm, understatement and implication carry meaning.
nearestNeighbour: CONVERSATIONAL IMPLICATURE. That is the meaning a listener derives beyond the literal words. This is the underlying account that explains why the derivation is possible at all. One is the mechanism, the other is its output.
discriminateScenario: Asked for a reference, a professor writes only that the candidate has excellent handwriting and was always punctual. Every word is true and nothing negative is stated. The committee understands the letter perfectly, and the candidate is not shortlisted.
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Common Ground in Conversation
oneSentence: Conversation works by building a shared store of what both people already know.
definition: Clark's account of conversation as a joint activity, in which participants continuously track what they can assume the other already knows. Every reference to a previous point, every shorthand, every it or that draws on this store. Where the store is thin, speakers must spell more out; where it is thick, a few words carry a great deal.

chains: speaker assumes shared ground that is not there

misconception: "It means finding things you have in common." That is rapport, which is a different thing. Common ground here is strictly about what each person can assume the other already knows, and two people with nothing in common can build plenty of it over one careful conversation.
nearestNeighbour: CURSE OF KNOWLEDGE. That is the bias that makes you unable to imagine not knowing what you know. This is the mechanism it damages: common ground is the thing being misjudged, and the curse is why the misjudgement happens.
discriminateScenario: Two teams meet about a shared project. One uses the phrase the migration throughout. The other team nods, and spends the following fortnight preparing for something different, because in their world that word refers to a different piece of work entirely.
praxisExercise:
CHECK THE GROUND

1. Before an important conversation, list the three terms you will rely on most.
2. For each, write what you are assuming the other person already knows.
3. Open by checking one of those assumptions out loud.
4. Note which one was wrong.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I start a conversation with someone outside my team, I will check one assumed term before relying on it."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Curse of Knowledge
oneSentence: Once you know something, you cannot imagine not knowing it.
definition: A bias in which knowing something makes it very hard to model the mind of someone who does not. It shows up whenever an expert explains their field: the steps they skip are invisible to them, because the knowledge that fills them is already in place. Demonstrated memorably in Elizabeth Newton's tapping study, where tappers wildly overestimated how often listeners would recognise the tune.

chains: the listener loses the thread where you skipped something without noticing

misconception: "It means experts are bad communicators." Expertise is not the problem; the invisibility of one's own knowledge is. A novice explaining something they half-know is often clearer, not because they know more but because the missing pieces are still visible to them.
nearestNeighbour: ILLUSION OF EXPLANATORY DEPTH. That one is about overestimating how well you understand something yourself. This one is about underestimating how much other people need told. One is a misjudgement of your own knowledge, the other a misjudgement of theirs.
discriminateScenario: A consultant presents to a new client and uses four abbreviations in the first two minutes without expanding any of them. The room nods along. Afterwards almost no one can describe what was proposed, and the consultant concludes that the client was not paying attention.
praxisExercise:
NAME WHAT YOU SKIPPED

1. Take something you are about to explain or publish.
2. Underline every term that would need explaining to someone outside your field.
3. For each, ask: did I actually explain it, or assume it?
4. Rewrite the three worst offenders.

COMMITMENT (if-then):
"When I write something for people outside my work, I will mark every assumed term before I send it."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Message Framing
oneSentence: The same fact persuades differently depending on how it is framed.
definition: Tversky and Kahneman showed that logically identical information produces different choices depending on presentation. A treatment described as having a ninety per cent survival rate is chosen more often than one with a ten per cent mortality rate. Framing is not a way of adding information. It is a choice about which true description of the same thing you put forward.

chains: it sets what counts as the baseline
the audience judges gains or losses against that baseline
the same facts lead to a different decision

misconception: "Framing is a polite word for spin." Spin involves saying things that are not true or hiding things that are. Every statement has a frame, including the plainest one available, so the choice is never between framing and not framing. It is between choosing the frame deliberately and letting it fall where it lands.
nearestNeighbour: ANCHORING. That is the pull of a specific number that was mentioned first, which then drags later estimates toward it. Framing is about which description of a situation is offered. One works through a numeric reference point, the other through the shape of the description.
discriminateScenario: A subscription team tests two versions of the same price. One reads twelve pounds a month, the other reads under forty pence a day. The cost is identical and both are accurate. The second converts markedly better, and nobody involved said anything untrue.
praxisExercise:
TWO TRUE FRAMES

1. Take something you need to communicate this week.
2. Write it in the frame that comes naturally.
3. Write a second version, equally true, from the opposite direction.
4. Choose deliberately, and note why.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I write anything meant to persuade, I will draft a second equally true framing before choosing."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Ethos, Pathos & Logos
oneSentence: Persuasion rests on character, feeling and reasoning together.
definition: Aristotle's account of the three available means of persuasion: ethos, the credibility of the speaker, pathos, the emotional state of the audience, and logos, the reasoning of the argument itself. His point was not that all three are equally weighted in every case, but that an argument relying on only one of them is doing a third of the available work.

chains: the audience has no reason to trust the speaker and no stake in the outcome
credibility makes it worth hearing, feeling makes it matter, reasoning makes it hold

misconception: "Ethos, pathos and logos are three styles, and you pick one." They are not alternatives. They are three things present in every act of persuasion, including when you neglect them. A speech with no attention to ethos still conveys an impression of its speaker, usually a worse one.
nearestNeighbour: ELABORATION LIKELIHOOD MODEL. That is a modern account of when audiences scrutinise an argument closely and when they go on surface cues instead. Aristotle's three are the materials of persuasion; the model is about the conditions under which each gets weight.
discriminateScenario: A researcher presents a genuinely strong case for a funding change. The reasoning is airtight. She does not mention that she ran the pilot herself, and she never says what happens to the families affected if nothing changes. The committee finds no fault with the argument and does not act on it.
praxisExercise:
THE MISSING THIRD

1. Take something you need to argue for.
2. Mark which of the three your draft leans on most.
3. Identify the one you have neglected entirely.
4. Add one sentence that supplies it, and no more.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I finish a persuasive draft, I will find the one of the three I neglected and add a single sentence for it."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Nonviolent Communication Framework
oneSentence: Separating what happened from how you felt, what you need and what you are asking.
definition: Rosenberg's framework splits a difficult statement into four parts: the observation, stripped of evaluation, the feeling it produced, the need underneath that feeling, and a specific request. Its work is done by the separation itself, since most conflict comes from these four arriving fused into a single accusation.

chains: observation, feeling, need and request arrive fused
there is something concrete to respond to
the conversation is about the request

misconception: "It is a softer, more polite way of complaining." Politeness is not the mechanism and the framework is often more direct than what it replaces, because it requires naming a specific request rather than hinting. A fused accusation delivered gently is still fused.
nearestNeighbour: AFFECT LABELING. That names the feeling and stops there, and it can be applied to the other person's feeling as well as your own. This framework includes naming a feeling as one of four steps, but the step that does the structural work is the specific request at the end.
discriminateScenario: After a third late delivery, Dan writes to his supplier that he is being treated as unimportant. The supplier replies defending their workload. Nothing changes. What Dan had wanted, and never said, was to be told on the day something would be late rather than finding out himself.
praxisExercise:
SPLIT IT INTO FOUR

1. Take something you need to raise with someone.
2. Write the observation with every evaluative word removed.
3. Write the feeling it produced, in one word.
4. Write the need underneath it.
5. Write one specific request that someone could say yes or no to.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I need to raise something difficult, I will write the specific request first and build the rest around it."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Positions vs. Interests
oneSentence: What someone demands is rarely the same as what they actually need.
definition: From Fisher and Ury's work on negotiation. A position is the stated demand. An interest is the underlying need the demand is meant to serve. Positions conflict far more often than interests do, which is why negotiations that trade positions tend to deadlock while negotiations that surface interests often find room neither side knew was there.

chains: the only move is splitting the difference
the interests often differ rather than conflict

misconception: "It means compromising, or meeting in the middle." Meeting in the middle is what you do when you are still trading positions. Finding interests often avoids compromise entirely, because the two parties turn out to want different things rather than the same thing in different amounts.
nearestNeighbour: BATNA. That is your best alternative if no agreement is reached, and it sets the point below which you should walk away. This is about understanding what either side is actually trying to achieve. One defines your floor, the other opens the space above it.
discriminateScenario: Two departments both insist on owning the new budget line, and neither will move. Eventually someone asks each what they are trying to do with it. One wants to guarantee a hire. The other wants to be able to show the spend in their own reporting. Both turn out to be possible.
praxisExercise:
FIND THE INTEREST

1. Take a disagreement you are currently stuck in.
2. Write both stated positions.
3. For each, ask: what is this meant to achieve? Keep asking until you reach something that is not itself a demand.
4. Look for an option that serves both answers.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When a negotiation deadlocks, I will ask what the other side is trying to achieve before offering any compromise."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Feynman Technique (Learning Heuristic)
oneSentence: Explain it simply, and the parts you cannot explain are what you do not know.
definition: A study method in which you write an explanation of a topic as though to someone with no background, find the points where the explanation fails or retreats into jargon, go back to the source for those points specifically, and repeat. Its value is diagnostic: it locates what is missing rather than filling it.

chains: the weak points refuse to be explained
you now know exactly what to go back for

misconception: "It is about making things simple." Simplicity is the test, not the goal. The output is not meant to be a simplified explanation you keep. The output is the list of places where you could not manage it, and those are the only part worth acting on.
nearestNeighbour: SELF EXPLANATION. That is explaining material to yourself as you study it, with no imagined audience and no requirement that it be plain. The imagined listener here is what forces jargon out, and jargon is where unexamined understanding hides.
discriminateScenario: Martin has read the chapter on cash flow three times and feels he has it. Asked to explain it to his sister over dinner, he gets two sentences in and finds he cannot say why a profitable business can run out of money. He had read that paragraph twice.
praxisExercise:
EXPLAIN IT TO ONE PERSON

1. Choose something you believe you understand.
2. Write an explanation for someone with no background, on one page, with no terms from the field.
3. Mark every point where you hesitated or reached for jargon.
4. Go back to the source for those points only.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I think I have understood something, I will write one page explaining it with no jargon and go back for whatever I could not write."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Ship of Theseus
oneSentence: If every part of a thing is replaced over time, is it still the same thing?
definition: The ship on which Theseus returned was preserved by the Athenians, who replaced each plank as it decayed until no original timber remained. Plutarch records that philosophers disagreed over whether it was still the same ship. The puzzle probes what we mean when we say something persists through change.

chains: competing answers (material continuity against continuity of form and function)

misconception: "It is a trick question with no answer." It is not unanswerable. It demonstrates that "the same thing" means different criteria in different contexts, and the puzzle's job is to expose which criterion you were silently using all along.
nearestNeighbour: THE SORITES PARADOX. The puzzle of the heap is also about vagueness under gradual change, but it concerns when a predicate stops applying, as in how many grains make a heap. This concerns the identity of one particular thing across time.
discriminateScenario: A company keeps its name and its logo but over fifteen years replaces every employee, relocates twice, changes its product line entirely and is sold to new owners. A long-standing customer insists it is not the same company any more. The current chief executive insists that it obviously is.
